### Response:
chosen: Primers are required in reverse transcription as it is a process where RNA is converted into DNA. Primers are needed because reverse transcriptase does not have a 5' to 3' exonuclease activity and hence cannot remove the RNA primer. Hence option D is incorrect.  A primer is a short nucleic acid sequence at the 5' end of each strand of DNA that serves as a starting point for DNA synthesis. It is necessary in DNA replication as it helps to reduce the probability of errors occurring in the copying process.  Possible sequences of primers are GATC or GTCG.  Primase is a type of RNA polymerase that is responsible for synthesising short RNA primers on the parent DNA strand before DNA replication begins. These primers are then removed after the lagging strand has been completed.  Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme that generates complementary DNA from a single-stranded RNA template. This enzyme is used in retroviruses such as HIV to produce viral DNA which can be integrated into the host genome.  Source: Lecture slides and textbook. rejected: D) is false because reverse transcription does not require primers as it is a process where RNA nucleotides are used to generate complementary DNA sequences. It occurs in retroviruses and is the mechanism for generating the provirus genome from the viral RNA. In eukaryotic cells, this process is catalyzed by reverse transcriptase. A) is true because a primer is needed to initiate DNA replication at the origin site of replication and the primer is synthesised by primase, a type of RNA polymerase. B) is true because the sequence of a primer should be shorter than 10 base pairs and contain G or C rich regions. This is because the primer must bind to the template strand and start the initiation of DNA replication. Primer binding requires the primer to form a hydrogen bond with the template strand. Hydrogen bonds are possible between G-C bases but not between A-T bases. Therefore, the primer needs to have more G or C bases so that it is able to bind to the template strand. C) is true because primase is a type of RNA polymerase which synthesises short RNA primers on the leading strand of the DNA. Primase also synthesise the RNA primers in the lagging strand of the DNA. The RNA primers are then removed and replaced with DNA primers by DNA polymerase I. These DNA primers are required for DNA ligase to seal the sugar phosphate backbone of Okazaki fragments together. This creates the continuous chain of DNA. Therefore, primase is responsible for the production of the primers. Source: Lecture slides and textbook. (2017). Sanfoundry. Another misconception is thinking that enzymes are rate limiting steps because some students may assume that enzymes work faster when they have more substrates available. However, enzyme activity is saturated meaning that the number of substrates doesn't change the rate of reaction. Instead, other factors such as temperature affect the rate of reaction. Lastly, some students may also confuse rate limiting steps with irreversible reactions. For example, in the production of ATP, oxygen is used up in the electron transport chain and cannot be recycled. So, the availability of oxygen is a rate limiting step in the electron transport chain. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books

Given question: Naomi decides on attending university for an entire week without consuming food. After 3-4 days which ketogenic process is NOT occurring? chosen: During starvation and low glucose levels the body uses ketones as fuel. However not all ketones produced will be used up by the brain and tissues. Some will be excreted in urine. This occurs because the kidneys cannot fully reabsorb the ketones due to their charge. The kidneys are very efficient at resorbing glucose from the filtrate but they are not so good at this with ketones. Hence some are lost.  Beta oxidation slows down during starvation because there is less carnitine available for transporting fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane. Hence ketogenesis takes over. In the liver acetyl co-A is turned into acetoacetate (2 acetyl co-A). Acetoacetate is unstable and spontaneously decarboxylates to form acetone. Two acetone molecules then fuse together to give the 3 carbon ketone body acetolactate. This process is called ketolysis and is one of two processes involved in ketogenesis. The other process is ketogenesis proper. In ketogenesis proper the acetoacetate is converted into two acetyl co-A molecules by a thiolytic cleavage reaction. This process involves niacin adenine dinucelotide (NAD) and the enzyme acyl co-A dehydrogenase. One NADH molecule is formed and one NAD+. The acetyl co-A are fused together to make 3-hydroxybutyrate or B-hydroxybutyrate. The latter is the main ketone body produced. It can cross the blood brain barrier and therefore be utilised by the brain and muscles. In order for this to occur the brain must be using glucose at a rate lower than 120g/day. The production of ketones occurs more rapidly than it is used up. Hence some are lost in the urine. An alternative name for ketosis is trioxocene bodies. Stem cells are totipotent, meaning they can differentiate into any type of specialised cell in the body. This loss of totipotency occurs as a result of a process called histone remodelling, whereby the expression of certain genes is altered. Whereas DNA ligase joins together the sugar-phosphate backbone of adjacent Okazaki fragments. Therefore, the newly synthesised DNA strand will not be shortened. Instead it will continue to grow until the entire sequence of bases have been copied over into the new strand. Furthermore, the removal of the RNA primers does not occur until after the entire DNA sequence has been copied over. In other words, the RNA primers are only removed when all the gaps on the DNA strands have been filled in. Hence, the newly synthesised DNA strand will not be shortened and will instead continue to grow in length.   I chose to make this statement false as I wanted to show how the addition of nucleotides occurs on both ends of the DNA strand during DNA replication. Moreover, I also wanted to highlight the importance of the removal of the RNA primer and how this step cannot occur until the entire DNA sequence has been copied over.  In order to achieve this, I thought making the statement seem true at first was the best approach. This way, readers would be able to think about what could possibly go wrong if the RNA primer was removed too early. For example, they might realise that the newly synthesised DNA strand would not be able to join up to the rest of the DNA sequence anymore. As a result, the newly synthesised DNA strand would become shorter and smaller. However, upon reading the explanation readers would see that this is not the case and that the removal of the RNA primer only occurs after the entire DNA sequence has been copied over. Therefore, the newly synthesised DNA strand will not be shortened but instead continue to grow in length. Thank you! :)  Source: Lecture notes from Case 14 - Chromosomal abnormalities in cancer.  See link for more information: https://www.studocu

Instead, DNA replication only occurs when nucleotides are added to the 3' strand with an available hydroxyl group. When the pH increases, the OH- groups on the bases are unable to dissociate into free protons and therefore cannot neutralise the negative charges on the sugar-phosphate backbone. This results in the formation of cyclic compounds between the bases. The more OH- groups present, the more cyclic compounds formed. Thus, increasing the pH of a solution containing RNA will enable MORE phosphates to form cyclic compounds. I think it's important to understand why this occurs so that we don't get confused when we see statements like "DNA is stable at high pH because it forms cyclic compounds". It's not that the cyclic compounds stabilise the DNA, but rather that the cyclic compounds form due to the stability of the DNA. Hopefully this question helps clear up any confusion! Topoisomerases are enzymes that control the topology of DNA or RNA molecules by breaking and reforming phosphodiester bonds in the backbone. They are important for many cellular processes including replication, transcription, recombination, chromosome segregation, and DNA repair. There are two classes of topoisomerases: type I and type II. Type I topoisomerases (including gyrase) cleave a single strand of DNA and then re-anneal it. rejected: The statement is false because nearly all eukaryotic organisms utilise histones to help compress their DNA and genetic material by forming nucleosomes. Prokaryotes do not have histones in their cells, which is one of the main reasons why their DNA is much less compact than eukaryotic DNA. This allows prokaryotes to replicate their DNA quickly.  Histones are positively charged proteins found in eukaryotic cells that assist in packaging DNA into chromosomes by binding to negatively charged DNA sequences. They are small proteins, typically about 100 amino acids long, and they can be highly alkaline. They were first discovered in 1882 by Albrecht Kossel. It was initially thought that histone proteins helped stabilize the shape of DNA by preventing its unwinding, but it has been shown that histones play an important role in gene regulation as well. The structure of histones is very similar to that of other proteins such as actin and tubulin. Histones are synthesized from mRNA by RNA polymerase II and then translated into proteins. These proteins are then assembled into subunits called nucleosomes, which form complexes called chromatin fibers. Chromatin fibers are formed when two strands of DNA twist around each other to form loops. When these loops are wrapped around histones, they create supercoils that make it difficult for enzymes to access genes within them. Supercoiling also makes it harder for transcription factors to bind to promoter regions on DNA molecules. Histones are tightly bound to DNA through electrostatic interactions between lysine residues on histones and phosphate groups on DNA. Histones can be removed from DNA using chemicals like EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid). Once removed, histones lose their ability to bind to DNA. Histones can be replaced with alternative proteins called histone variants. Histone variants include H3A, H4A, H5B, H6C, H7D, H8E, H9F, H10G, H11H, H12I, H13J, H14K, H15L, H16M, H17N, H18O, H19P
